\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The resolution question}

Every equivalence relation on mathematical objects is a decision about which differences matter. In the theory of transition systems there are two canonical candidates. \emph{Isomorphism} says two systems are the same when there is a structure-preserving bijection between them: sameness of shape. \emph{Bisimulation} says they are the same when a copycat relation lets each mirror the other's moves indefinitely: sameness of behaviour.

Between these lies a third, purely logical notion: two pointed systems are the same when no sentence of a fixed observational language separates them. Fix the language and you fix an equivalence. The \emph{resolution question} asks which structural equivalence a given language induces.

For ordinary modal logic on image-finite systems the classical answer is bisimulation, and our first task is to prove this in the present setting. The more interesting question is the \emph{shape of the residue}: exactly what structure does isomorphism see that no modal observation can?

\subsection{The conjecture and its fate}

The natural conjecture is that the residue is \emph{multiplicity}. Modal logic has no counting quantifier: it can say ``some successor is red'' and ``every successor is red'' but not ``exactly two successors are red''. Duplicating a successor is invisible to it, whereas isomorphism preserves out-degree exactly. So it is tempting to conjecture:

\begin{quote}
On image-finite transition systems, every interpretation invariant under all modal observations factors through bisimulation classes but need not factor through isomorphism classes, and the gap is characterized by multiplicity-sensitive observations.
\end{quote}

We prove the first two clauses and refute the third. The counterexample --- a shared diamond versus its unravelling --- is bisimilar, out-degree-matched at every related pair, and non-isomorphic. Counting is a \emph{proper} refinement of behaviour and a \emph{proper} coarsening of shape.

\subsection{The setting}

\begin{definition}[Descending tag-indexed frame]
A \emph{frame} is a function $R:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\to\{\top,\bot\}$, written $R\,i\,m\,n$ and read ``at tag $i$, world $m$ is linked to world $n$''. The \emph{step relation} is
\[
\Step_R(i,m,n) \;:\iff\; n<m \;\wedge\; R\,i\,m\,n .
\]
A \emph{valuation} is $V:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\to\{\top,\bot\}$, with $V\,m\,p$ read ``the atom $p$ holds at world $m$''. A \emph{pointed model} is a triple $(R,V,m)$.
\end{definition}

The strict inequality $n<m$ is the whole design.

\begin{lemma}[Image-finiteness]
The successors of $m$ at tag $i$ are exactly the members of the finite list obtained by filtering $\{0,\dots,m-1\}$ by $R\,i\,m\,{-}$. In particular a world has at most $m$ successors at each tag.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Converse well-foundedness]
Every step strictly decreases the world index, so no infinite forward path exists; the \emph{height} of a world $m$ is at most $m$.
\end{lemma}

Both are immediate; their consequences are not. Image-finiteness powers the Hennessy--Milner argument of \S3, converse well-foundedness the collapse threshold of \S8.

\begin{definition}[Language and semantics]
Formulas are generated by
\[
a ::= \bot \;\mid\; p \;\mid\; a\to a \;\mid\; \Box_i a \qquad (p,i\in\mathbb{N}).
\]
Satisfaction $(R,V,m)\models a$ is defined by recursion: $\bot$ never holds; $p$ holds iff $V\,m\,p$; $a\to b$ holds iff $a$ fails or $b$ holds; and
\[
(R,V,m)\models\Box_i a \iff \forall n,\; \Step_R(i,m,n) \Rightarrow (R,V,n)\models a .
\]
We abbreviate $\neg a:=a\to\bot$, $\top:=\bot\to\bot$, $a\wedge b:=\neg(a\to\neg b)$, $\Diamond_i a := \neg\Box_i\neg a$. The \emph{box depth} $\bd(a)$ counts maximal box nesting, and $\Box^j_i\bot$ is the $j$-fold iterate of $\Box_i$ applied to $\bot$.
\end{definition}

The language has only $\bot$, atoms, $\to$ and boxes as primitives, so finite conjunction must be \emph{defined} --- as the fold of the derived binary conjunction over a list, with $\top$ as unit --- and its semantics proved: the conjunction of a list is true at $m$ iff every member is. No infinitary conjunction appears anywhere. The tags are genuinely multi-modal but cause no difficulty: every argument is carried out one tag at a time.

\section{Equivalences and invariants}

\begin{definition}[Bisimulation]
A relation $E\subseteq\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ is a \emph{bisimulation} between $(R,V)$ and $(R',V')$ when for all $m\mathrel{E}n$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{(atoms)} $V\,m\,p = V'\,n\,p$ for every atom $p$;
\item \emph{(forth)} for every tag $i$ and every $m'$ with $\Step_R(i,m,m')$ there is $n'$ with $\Step_{R'}(i,n,n')$ and $m'\mathrel{E}n'$;
\item \emph{(back)} for every tag $i$ and every $n'$ with $\Step_{R'}(i,n,n')$ there is $m'$ with $\Step_R(i,m,m')$ and $m'\mathrel{E}n'$.
\end{enumerate}
Pointed models are \emph{bisimilar}, $(R,V,m)\sim(R',V',n)$, when some bisimulation relates $m$ to $n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Modal equivalence]
$(R,V,m)\equiv(R',V',n)$ when $(R,V,m)\models a \iff (R',V',n)\models a$ for every formula $a$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
Bisimilarity is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Equality is a bisimulation. The converse of a bisimulation is a bisimulation with forth and back exchanged. The relational composite $E;F$ of two bisimulations is a bisimulation: a forth-step is matched through the intermediate model in two stages, and dually for back.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Reachability and pointed isomorphism]
$\Reach_R(r)$ is the least set containing $r$ and closed under steps at all tags. A \emph{pointed isomorphism} $F:(R,V,r)\cong(R',V',r')$ consists of maps $f,g:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ with $f(r)=r'$ and $g(r')=r$, such that $f$ maps $\Reach_R(r)$ into $\Reach_{R'}(r')$ and $g$ conversely, $g\circ f$ is the identity on $\Reach_R(r)$ and $f\circ g$ on $\Reach_{R'}(r')$, both maps preserve steps at every tag on reachable worlds, and $f$ preserves atoms on reachable worlds.
\end{definition}

This is deliberately a \emph{weak} notion: it constrains only the generated submodels. Consequently non-existence statements about pointed isomorphisms are correspondingly strong.

\begin{definition}[Interpretations and invariance]
An \emph{interpretation} with values in $\alpha$ assigns to each pointed model $(R,V,m)$ an element $I(R,V,m)\in\alpha$. It is \emph{modally invariant} if $\equiv$ implies equality of values; \emph{bisimulation invariant} if $\sim$ does; \emph{isomorphism invariant} if the existence of a pointed isomorphism does; and \emph{depth-$k$ invariant} if agreement on all formulas of box depth $\le k$ does. The corresponding classes are $\ModalInv$, $\BisimInv$, $\IsoInv$, $\DepthInv_k$.
\end{definition}

A \emph{finer} equivalence is a \emph{weaker} invariance requirement, so inclusions among invariance classes run opposite to inclusions among equivalences.

\begin{definition}[Out-degree]
$\deg_R(j,m):=\#\{\,n<m : R\,j\,m\,n\,\}$, the paradigmatic multiplicity-sensitive observation, with associated interpretation $I_{\deg,j}(R,V,m):=\deg_R(j,m)$.
\end{definition}

\section{The Hennessy--Milner theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Bisimulation invariance of modal truth]
Let $E$ be a bisimulation between $(R,V)$ and $(R',V')$. Then for every formula $a$ and every $m\mathrel{E}n$, $(R,V,m)\models a \iff (R',V',n)\models a$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $a$. The case $\bot$ is trivial, atoms are the atom clause, implication is immediate. For $\Box_i b$: assume it holds at $m$ and let $n'$ be an $i$-successor of $n$; by \emph{back} there is an $i$-successor $m'$ of $m$ with $m'\mathrel{E}n'$, where $b$ holds, hence by induction $b$ holds at $n'$. The converse uses \emph{forth}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Bisimilar pointed models are modally equivalent.
\end{corollary}

\begin{lemma}[Forth for modal equivalence]\label{lem:forth}
Suppose $(R,V,m)\equiv(R',V',n)$ and $\Step_R(i,m,m')$. Then there is $n'$ with $\Step_{R'}(i,n,n')$ and $(R,V,m')\equiv(R',V',n')$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Suppose not. For each $i$-successor $n'$ of $n$ choose a formula $a_{n'}$ true at $m'$ and false at $n'$ (negating if necessary); for indices that are not successors of $n$, set $a_{n'}:=\top$. All successors of $n$ lie below $n$, so we may form the finite conjunction $A:=\bigwedge_{n'<n} a_{n'}$. Then $A$ is true at $m'$, and false at every $i$-successor $n'$ of $n$. Hence $\Box_i\neg A$ holds at $n$, so by modal equivalence at $m$; but $m'$ is an $i$-successor of $m$ where $A$ is true --- a contradiction.
\end{proof}

The choice of range $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ rather than ``the set of successors'' keeps the construction finite and explicit; padding with $\top$ costs nothing.

\begin{theorem}[Hennessy--Milner]\label{thm:hm}
Modal equivalence is itself a bisimulation. Consequently
\[
(R,V,m)\sim(R',V',n) \iff (R,V,m)\equiv(R',V',n).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The atom clause is modal equivalence applied to atoms; \emph{forth} is Lemma~\ref{lem:forth}; \emph{back} is Lemma~\ref{lem:forth} applied to the symmetric modal equivalence and transported back. The displayed equivalence follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Factorization through bisimulation classes]\label{thm:fact}
$\ModalInv = \BisimInv$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Modal theory]
$\Theta(R,V,m):=\{\,a : (R,V,m)\models a\,\}$, viewed as an interpretation.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Universality of the modal theory]
$\Theta$ is modally invariant, and every modally invariant interpretation factors through it: if $\Theta(R,V,m)=\Theta(R',V',n)$ then $I(R,V,m)=I(R',V',n)$ for every modally invariant $I$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Equality of modal theories \emph{is} modal equivalence.
\end{proof}

\section{The depth ladder}

\begin{definition}
$(R,V,m)\equiv_k(R',V',n)$ --- \emph{depth-$k$ equivalence} --- when the pointed models agree on every formula of box depth at most $k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Modal equivalence is the limit]
$(R,V,m)\equiv(R',V',n)$ iff $(R,V,m)\equiv_k(R',V',n)$ for every $k$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Right to left: given $a$, apply the hypothesis at $k=\bd(a)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[The chain]
$\mathrm{chain}\,i\,m\,n :\iff n+1=m$, at every tag; all atoms hold everywhere.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Modal theory of the chain]\label{lem:chain}
In the chain, $\Box^j_i\bot$ holds at $m$ iff $m<j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $j$. For $j=0$ the formula is $\bot$. For $j+1$: it holds at $0$ vacuously and at $p+1$ iff $\Box^j_i\bot$ holds at $p$, i.e. iff $p<j$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:chaindepth}
If $k\le m$ and $k\le n$ then $(\mathrm{chain},m)\equiv_k(\mathrm{chain},n)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The family $E_l:=\{(p,q):l\le p \wedge l\le q\}$ is a depth-graded (bounded) bisimulation: a step from $p$ at level $l+1$ lands at $p-1$, matched by $q\to q-1$, with $l\le p-1$ and $l\le q-1$. The transfer lemma for bounded bisimulations transports all formulas of depth $\le k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sep}
$(\mathrm{chain},k)\not\equiv_{k+1}(\mathrm{chain},k+1)$, via $\Box^{k+1}\bot$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{definition}[Height interpretation]
$I_{\mathrm{ht},j}(R,V,m)$ is the truth value of $\Box^j_0\bot$ at $(R,V,m)$; it is depth-$j$ invariant by construction.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Strictness of every rung]
For every $k$, $\DepthInv_k\subseteq\DepthInv_{k+1}$, and the inclusion is strict: $I_{\mathrm{ht},k+1}$ is depth-$(k+1)$ invariant but not depth-$k$ invariant.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The chain worlds $k$ and $k+1$ are depth-$k$ equivalent by Lemma~\ref{lem:chaindepth} but assign different values to $I_{\mathrm{ht},k+1}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:chain}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No finite depth reaches bisimulation]
For every $k$, $\DepthInv_k\subsetneq\ModalInv$: the modal theory is modally invariant but not depth-$k$ invariant.
\end{theorem}

\section{The multiplicity gap}

\begin{definition}[Multiplicity frame]
The frame $M$ has, at every tag, the edges
\[
1\to0,\qquad 2\to0,\qquad 3\to1,\quad 3\to2,\qquad 4\to1,
\]
and the constant valuation making every atom true everywhere.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:multcls}
Let $c(m):=1$ for $m\in\{1,2\}$, $2$ for $m\in\{3,4\}$, and $0$ otherwise. The kernel $\{(m,n):c(m)=c(n)\}$ is a bisimulation of $M$ with itself.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
A step out of $1$ or $2$ goes to $0$, and every world of class $1$ has a step to $0$; a step out of $3$ or $4$ goes to a world of class $1$, and every world of class $2$ has a step to $1$. \emph{Back} follows by symmetry of the kernel.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
$(M,3)\sim(M,4)$, hence $(M,3)\equiv(M,4)$: no modal formula of any depth separates a world with two behaviourally identical successors from one with a single successor.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Out-degree is an isomorphism invariant]\label{lem:degiso}
If $F:(R,V,r)\cong(R',V',r')$ then $\deg_R(j,r)=\deg_{R'}(j,r')$ for every tag $j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The forward map $f$ sends successors of $r$ to successors of $r'$, is injective on reachable worlds, and is surjective onto the successors of $r'$ (pull back along $g$). A bijection of successor sets gives equality of cardinalities.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
There is no pointed isomorphism $(M,3)\cong(M,4)$, since $\deg_M(0,3)=2$ and $\deg_M(0,4)=1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The multiplicity gap]
$\BisimInv\subsetneq\IsoInv$. Precisely: every bisimulation-invariant interpretation is isomorphism invariant, because isomorphic pointed models are bisimilar; and $I_{\deg,0}$ is isomorphism invariant but not bisimulation invariant.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch of the first clause]
Given $F:(R,V,r)\cong(R',V',r')$, the relation $\{(m,f(m)) : m\in\Reach_R(r)\}$ is a bisimulation: atoms are preserved by hypothesis, \emph{forth} is step preservation of $f$, and \emph{back} is obtained by pulling a step back along $g$ and using the two inversion identities on reachable worlds.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The two gaps are independent]
For every $k$, the pair $(M,3),(M,4)$ is depth-$k$ equivalent, yet separated by the multiplicity observation. The top gap is therefore not a limit of the finite gaps of \S4.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Full resolution hierarchy]
For every $k$,
\[
\DepthInv_0\subsetneq\DepthInv_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\DepthInv_k\subsetneq\ModalInv=\BisimInv\subsetneq\IsoInv,
\]
with the height observations $\Box^{k+1}\bot$ separating the finite layers and the out-degree separating the top one.
\end{theorem}

\section{Multiplicity does not close the gap}

\begin{definition}[Shared diamond and unravelling]
At every tag, the \emph{shared diamond} $S$ has edges $5\to3$, $5\to4$, $3\to1$, $4\to1$; the \emph{unravelling} $T$ has edges $5\to3$, $5\to4$, $3\to1$, $4\to2$. Both carry the constant valuation. From the root $5$, the diamond reaches four worlds, the tree five.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sharcls}
Let $s(m):=2$ for $m=5$, $1$ for $m\in\{3,4\}$, and $0$ otherwise. Then $\{(m,n):s(m)=s(n)\}$ is a bisimulation between $S$ and $T$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
\emph{Forth}: a step out of $5$ in $S$ lands in $\{3,4\}$, matched by $5\to3$ in $T$ (class $1$); a step out of $3$ or $4$ in $S$ lands at $1$ (class $0$), matched in $T$ by $3\to1$ or $4\to2$, both of class $0$. \emph{Back} is symmetric.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Behavioural identity]
$(S,5)\sim(T,5)$, hence $(S,5)\equiv(T,5)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Multiplicity match]\label{thm:multmatch}
For all $m,n$ with $s(m)=s(n)$ and every tag $i$, $\deg_S(i,m)=\deg_T(i,n)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Neither frame depends on the tag. Class $2$ forces $m=n=5$, degrees $2$ and $2$. Class $1$ forces $m,n\in\{3,4\}$, all four degrees $1$. Class $0$ forces $m,n\notin\{3,4,5\}$, where neither frame has an outgoing edge, so both degrees are $0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[No pointed isomorphism]\label{thm:noiso}
There is no pointed isomorphism $(S,5)\cong(T,5)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $g$ be the backward map, so $g(5)=5$. The tree steps $5\to3$ and $5\to4$ pull back to steps $5\to g(3)$ and $5\to g(4)$ in the diamond, whose only successors of $5$ are $3$ and $4$; hence $g(3),g(4)\in\{3,4\}$. The tree step $3\to1$ pulls back to $g(3)\to g(1)$, and both $3$ and $4$ have unique successor $1$ in the diamond, so $g(1)=1$; identically $g(2)=1$. But $g$ is injective on reachable worlds and $1\ne2$ are both reachable.
\end{proof}

The argument uses only injectivity on reachable worlds and backward step preservation, so it is robust to substantial weakening of the notion of isomorphism.

\begin{theorem}[Refutation]
There exist pointed models that are simultaneously bisimilar (hence modally indistinguishable at every depth) and multiplicity-matched (corresponding worlds have equal out-degrees at every tag), and yet not isomorphic. Hence the clause ``the gap is characterized by multiplicity-sensitive observations'' is false.
\end{theorem}

\begin{discussion}
Both witnesses are quotients: $M$ duplicates a successor, while $S$ is the quotient of $T$ identifying its two behaviourally equal leaves. The first operation changes out-degree; the second does not. The residual invisible structure is \emph{sharing} --- whether behaviourally equal successors are literally the same world --- with the number of reachable worlds ($4$ versus $5$) as a convenient numerical proxy: an isomorphism invariant that is neither a modal nor a multiplicity invariant.
\end{discussion}

\begin{theorem}[Two-step ladder]
The resolution ladder above bisimulation has at least two proper steps,
\[
\text{bisimulation} \;\subsetneq\; \text{bisimulation}+\text{multiplicity} \;\subsetneq\; \text{isomorphism},
\]
witnessed by $(M,3)$ versus $(M,4)$ and by $(S,5)$ versus $(T,5)$ respectively; and the nominal language of \S7 collapses the whole ladder to equality.
\end{theorem}

\section{What closes the gap: names, and their price}

\subsection{Nominals}

\begin{definition}[Nominal valuation]
$V_{\mathrm{nom}}\,m\,p := [\,m=p\,]$: the atom $p$ is true exactly at world $p$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Nominals force equality]\label{thm:nom}
If $(R,V_{\mathrm{nom}},m)\equiv(R',V_{\mathrm{nom}},n)$ then $m=n$. Only the atomic fragment is used.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The atom $m$ is true at $m$; by modal equivalence it is true at $n$; by definition $n=m$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Over a nominal valuation on a fixed frame, modally equivalent pointed models are isomorphic --- indeed identical. Consequently every interpretation whatsoever, including the multiplicity observation, is modally invariant on such a frame.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The naming budget}

\begin{definition}[Binary naming]
$V_{\mathrm{bin}}\,m\,p :=$ the $p$-th bit of $m$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Logarithmic sufficiency]
Let $m,n<2^k$ agree on the atoms $0,\dots,k-1$ under $V_{\mathrm{bin}}$. Then $m=n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Two naturals are equal iff all their bits agree. For $p<k$ the bits agree by hypothesis; for $p\ge k$ both numbers are below $2^k\le 2^p$, so both bits vanish.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
For $m,n<2^k$, modal equivalence over $V_{\mathrm{bin}}$ on a fixed frame implies $m=n$, hence a pointed isomorphism, and the out-degree observation becomes modally invariant on that truncation. The collapse occurs already at box depth $0$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Matching lower bound]
Let $2^k\le N$ and let $V$ be \emph{any} valuation. Then there exist distinct $m,n\le N$ with $V\,m\,p = V\,n\,p$ for all $p<k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The map sending a world to its atomic $k$-type has domain of size $\ge 2^k+1$ and codomain $\{\top,\bot\}^k$ of size $2^k$. Pigeonhole.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Naming threshold]
With $k$ atoms: the binary valuation separates all worlds below $2^k$ atomically, so modal equivalence there is equality and every interpretation becomes modally invariant; and once the truncation level reaches $2^k$, no valuation separates all worlds atomically. Hence $\lceil\log_2 N\rceil$ atoms is the exact budget at which the observational hierarchy collapses.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}[Scope of the lower bound]
The lower bound concerns the \emph{atomic} fragment. It does not claim that $k$ atoms together with modalities cannot separate more worlds --- a frame may separate worlds structurally, as the chain does with no atoms at all. The correct reading is that \emph{naming}, as opposed to \emph{observing behaviour}, is impossible below the logarithmic budget.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[The gap requires atom poverty]
The witnesses of \S\S5--6 both carry the constant valuation, and this is no accident: a frame whose valuation separates its worlds atomically admits no bisimulation/isomorphism gap at all.
\end{theorem}

\section{Where the depth ladder stops}

\begin{definition}[Trimming]
Define $\tr_k(a)$ by recursion: $\tr_k(\bot)=\bot$; $\tr_k(p)=p$; $\tr_k(a\to b)=\tr_k(a)\to\tr_k(b)$; $\tr_0(\Box_i a)=\top$; $\tr_{k+1}(\Box_i a)=\Box_i\tr_k(a)$. Every box nested deeper than $k$ is replaced by verum.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}
$\bd(\tr_k(a))\le k$ for every $a$ and $k$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Trimming is invisible below its level]\label{lem:trim}
If $m\le k$ then $(R,V,m)\models\tr_k(a) \iff (R,V,m)\models a$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $a$, generalizing over $k$ and $m$. For $\Box_i b$ with $k=0$ we have $m=0$, which has no successors, so both $\Box_i b$ and $\top$ hold vacuously. For $k=k'+1$, every successor $n$ of $m$ satisfies $n<m\le k'+1$, hence $n\le k'$, and the induction hypothesis applies at level $k'$; the two box clauses match successor by successor.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Collapse threshold]
If $m\le k$, $n\le k$ and $(R,V,m)\equiv_k(R',V',n)$, then $(R,V,m)\equiv(R',V',n)$, and hence by Theorem~\ref{thm:hm} the two pointed models are bisimilar.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For arbitrary $a$, the truth value of $a$ at $m$ equals that of $\tr_k(a)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:trim}, likewise at $n$; and $\tr_k(a)$ has depth $\le k$, so the two values agree by hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
For $m,n\le k$, bisimilarity, modal equivalence and depth-$k$ equivalence coincide.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness]
In the chain, worlds $N$ and $N+1$ are depth-$N$ equivalent but not depth-$(N+1)$ equivalent, whereas depth $N+1$ does suffice for worlds of height at most $N+1$. On a model of height $N$ the Hennessy--Milner interrogation therefore needs exactly $N$ rounds in the worst case.
\end{theorem}

The infinite ladder is thus infinite only because the truncation level is unbounded.

\section{Proof-theoretic shadow: theories cannot see sharing}

Descending frames validate the L\"ob axiom, so their validity theories are G\"odel--L\"ob-style provability logics. Fix a truncation level $N$ and let $\Th_N(R,V)$ be the theory whose theorems are exactly the formulas valid at every world $m\le N$. A standard measure of strength is the family of \emph{depth-restricted reflection rules}: $\Th$ satisfies $\Refl(d,i)$ when, for every $a$ of box depth $\le d$, provability of $\Box_i a$ entails provability of $a$.

\begin{theorem}[Theory transfer along bisimulation]\label{thm:transfer}
Let $E$ be a bisimulation between $(R,V)$ and $(R',V')$ such that every $m\le N$ is $E$-related to some $n\le N'$ and conversely. Then $\Th_N(R,V)$ and $\Th_{N'}(R',V')$ prove exactly the same formulas.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Provability in a truncated theory is validity below the truncation. Given a formula provable on the left and $n\le N'$, choose a related $m\le N$; the formula's truth value at $n$ matches its value at $m$, where it is true. Symmetrically for the converse.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Under the same hypotheses the two theories satisfy exactly the same depth-restricted reflection rules; the entire reflection-depth spectrum is a bisimulation invariant.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Deduction cannot detect sharing]
For every truncation level $N$, the shared diamond and its unravelling have literally the same truncated theory and the same reflection spectrum, agree on all out-degrees, and are not isomorphic.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The class kernel of Lemma~\ref{lem:sharcls} relates each world to itself, so the coverage hypotheses hold trivially at every $N$; combine with Theorems~\ref{thm:multmatch} and~\ref{thm:noiso}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
In the multiplicity frame, the roots $3$ and $4$ have out-degrees $2$ and $1$ and are modally, hence proof-theoretically, indistinguishable.
\end{theorem}

Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer} requires only \emph{coverage}, not a bijection, so the truncated theory is even coarser than bisimilarity of pointed models: it sees only the \emph{set} of behaviours present below the truncation, not their multiplicities. Coverage is nevertheless necessary --- without it a frame with more worlds can validate strictly fewer formulas.

\section{Algorithms}

\textbf{Partition refinement for bisimilarity.} To compute bisimilarity on the worlds $0,\dots,N$ of a descending frame, start from the partition by atomic type (over a finite atom set) and repeatedly split a block whenever two of its members have, for some tag, different sets of successor blocks. Each round is one Ehrenfeucht--Fra\"iss\'e round; at most $N$ rounds are needed. A naive implementation with $N$ worlds, $t$ tags and $E$ edges runs in $O(N\cdot t\cdot E)$; the Paige--Tarjan strategy of splitting by the smaller half improves this to $O(E\log N)$. The output blocks are exactly the modal-equivalence classes.

\textbf{Depth-graded refinement.} Halting after $k$ rounds yields exactly the depth-$k$ equivalence classes. On the chain truncated at $N$, round $k$ separates world $k$ from everything above it, and the partitions refine strictly for exactly $N$ rounds --- a computational reading of the sharpness theorem.

\textbf{Separating-formula synthesis.} When refinement splits two worlds, the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:forth} is constructive: if $m$ has a successor $m'$ inequivalent to every successor of $n$, take $A$ to be the conjunction of the separating formulas for $m'$ against each successor of $n$, and return $\Diamond_i A$; the dual case returns the negation of the formula for the swapped pair. The recursion terminates because it descends in the frame, and the depth of the returned formula is bounded by the round at which refinement split the two worlds.

Running these on the witnesses reproduces the theorems: worlds $3$ and $4$ of the multiplicity frame stay in one block at every round, as do the two roots of the diamond and its unravelling, while exhaustive enumeration of the $6560$ formulas over one atom and one tag built in three layers finds no separating formula for either witness pair, and many for controls such as the chain worlds $1$ and $2$.

\section{Applications}

\textbf{Process algebra and verification.} The factorization theorem is a licence: any verification quantity definable by modal observation may be computed on any bisimilar model, in particular the smallest. Partition refinement is therefore a sound minimization pre-pass. The refutation is the corresponding warning: state count is not recoverable from behaviour even after the language is enriched with counting.

\textbf{Term graphs and sharing.} The distinction between the shared diamond and its unravelling is exactly that between a term graph with sharing and the tree it denotes. The two denote the same value, are different objects, and no arity or degree information detects the difference --- a precise statement of why sharing is a \emph{space} property rather than a semantic one.

\textbf{Epistemic and hybrid logic.} The nominal collapse explains in one line why hybrid logic with nominals defines frame properties beyond pure modal logic: naming is a total enrichment, worth exactly $\log_2 N$ bits, which suggests reading fragments of hybrid logic as \emph{partial} naming budgets.

\textbf{Provability logic.} The transfer theorems say the whole spectrum of reflection strength of a truncated frame theory is behavioural: deductive strength cannot distinguish structures that no observer distinguishes.

\section{Discussion and future work}

The conjecture has been resolved with a split verdict. Its positive half --- that modal invariance factors exactly through bisimulation classes --- is a theorem, in the strong form that the modal theory is a universal modally invariant interpretation. Its negative half is \emph{true but incomplete}: multiplicity is a genuine, genuinely non-modal gap, but adding it to bisimulation still falls strictly short of isomorphism. The obstruction is sharing.

Three structural lessons emerge. First, the hierarchy is two-dimensional: below bisimulation the gaps are about \emph{depth} of nesting, above it about \emph{identity} of destinations, and the two dimensions are independent. Second, the whole phenomenon is atom-relative, with $\lceil\log_2 N\rceil$ atoms dissolving every gap in the atomic fragment; all witnesses of a gap must be atom-poor, and they are. Third, interrogation length equals height, with the sharp bound realized by the chain.

Promising directions:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Axiomatize ``bisimulation $+$ multiplicity''.} Graded modal logic, with counting modalities $\Diamond^{\ge n}$, is the obvious candidate for the intermediate level; one would like a Hennessy--Milner theorem for it and an exact characterization of the second gap by a sharing invariant.
\item \textbf{A quantitative sharing invariant.} The reachable-world count is crude. A canonical candidate is the \emph{sharing defect}: the difference between the size of the depth-$k$ unravelling and the size of the model. Whether this, or the lattice of quotients between a model and its minimal bisimilar quotient, is a complete invariant is open.
\item \textbf{Partial naming budgets.} Between the constant valuation and full naming lies a graded family. Does resolution vary monotonically with the budget, and is there a threshold phenomenon?
\item \textbf{Beyond descending frames.} Descent buys image-finiteness and converse well-foundedness for free. Isolating which results survive under image-finiteness alone (Hennessy--Milner does; the collapse threshold does not, as it uses height) would separate the logical facts from the structural ones.
\item \textbf{Effective sharing detection.} Given two bisimilar finite models, decide isomorphism of their generated submodels: graph isomorphism restricted to a bisimulation class, plausibly tractable, and of practical value in term-graph rewriting.
\end{itemize}

"""
Bisimulation versus isomorphism as semantic resolution
=======================================================

Numerical demonstration of the results on descending tag-indexed frames.

Setting
-------
Worlds are natural numbers.  A frame is a family of relations indexed by a *tag*,
and a world `m` may step, at tag `i`, only to worlds `n < m`.  This makes every
frame image-finite (a world has at most `m` successors) and converse
well-founded (the height of world `m` is at most `m`).

The observational language is multi-modal:

    a ::= bot | atom p | a -> a | Box_i a

with `Box_i a` true at `m` iff every `i`-successor of `m` satisfies `a`.

What this script verifies
-------------------------
1.  Hennessy-Milner: partition refinement (bisimilarity) agrees exactly with
    exhaustive formula enumeration (modal equivalence) on all witness frames.
2.  The multiplicity gap: worlds 3 and 4 of the frame
        1 -> 0, 2 -> 0, 3 -> 1, 3 -> 2, 4 -> 1
    are bisimilar but have out-degrees 2 and 1, hence are not isomorphic.
3.  Refutation of the multiplicity conjecture: the shared diamond
        5 -> 3, 5 -> 4, 3 -> 1, 4 -> 1
    and its unravelling
        5 -> 3, 5 -> 4, 3 -> 1, 4 -> 2
    are bisimilar, out-degree matched at every related pair, and NOT isomorphic
    (4 vs 5 reachable worlds).
4.  The depth ladder in the chain frame `m + 1 -> m`: worlds k and k+1 agree up
    to depth k and are separated at depth k+1 by the height formula Box^(k+1) bot.
5.  The collapse threshold: on worlds of height <= k, depth-k agreement already
    implies full modal equivalence.
6.  The naming budget: k atoms of the binary naming valuation separate all
    worlds below 2^k atomically, and 2^k + 1 worlds always collide.

Run with:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from itertools import combinations
from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Set, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Frames, valuations, formulas, semantics
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Edge = Tuple[int, int, int]  # (tag, source, target)

Valuation = Callable[[int, int], bool]  # (world, atom) -> truth value


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Frame:
    """A descending tag-indexed frame given by an explicit finite edge set.

    Only edges with ``target < source`` are retained: the descending condition
    is enforced structurally, so image-finiteness and converse well-foundedness
    hold by construction.
    """

    name: str
    edges: FrozenSet[Edge]

    @staticmethod
    def of(name: str, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> "Frame":
        kept = frozenset((i, m, n) for (i, m, n) in edges if n < m)
        return Frame(name, kept)

    def successors(self, tag: int, world: int) -> List[int]:
        """The i-successors of a world, in increasing order."""
        return sorted(n for (i, m, n) in self.edges if i == tag and m == world)

    def out_degree(self, tag: int, world: int) -> int:
        """The multiplicity-sensitive observation: number of successors."""
        return len(self.successors(tag, world))

    def tags(self) -> List[int]:
        return sorted({i for (i, _, _) in self.edges}) or [0]

    def reachable(self, root: int) -> Set[int]:
        """Worlds reachable from ``root`` along steps of arbitrary tags."""
        seen: Set[int] = {root}
        frontier = [root]
        while frontier:
            m = frontier.pop()
            for i in self.tags():
                for n in self.successors(i, m):
                    if n not in seen:
                        seen.add(n)
                        frontier.append(n)
        return seen

    def height(self, world: int) -> int:
        """Length of the longest path leaving ``world`` (bounded by ``world``)."""
        best = 0
        for i in self.tags():
            for n in self.successors(i, world):
                best = max(best, 1 + self.height(n))
        return best


# --- formulas -------------------------------------------------------------

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Bot:
    pass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Atom:
    p: int


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Imp:
    a: "Formula"
    b: "Formula"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Box:
    tag: int
    a: "Formula"


Formula = object  # one of Bot, Atom, Imp, Box


def box_depth(a: Formula) -> int:
    """Maximal nesting of boxes."""
    if isinstance(a, (Bot, Atom)):
        return 0
    if isinstance(a, Imp):
        return max(box_depth(a.a), box_depth(a.b))
    if isinstance(a, Box):
        return 1 + box_depth(a.a)
    raise TypeError(a)


def show(a: Formula) -> str:
    if isinstance(a, Bot):
        return "⊥"
    if isinstance(a, Atom):
        return f"p{a.p}"
    if isinstance(a, Imp):
        if isinstance(a.b, Bot):
            return f"¬({show(a.a)})"
        return f"({show(a.a)} → {show(a.b)})"
    if isinstance(a, Box):
        return f"□{a.tag}({show(a.a)})"
    raise TypeError(a)


def sat(frame: Frame, val: Valuation, world: int, a: Formula) -> bool:
    """Satisfaction of a formula at a world."""
    if isinstance(a, Bot):
        return False
    if isinstance(a, Atom):
        return val(world, a.p)
    if isinstance(a, Imp):
        return (not sat(frame, val, world, a.a)) or sat(frame, val, world, a.b)
    if isinstance(a, Box):
        return all(sat(frame, val, n, a.a) for n in frame.successors(a.tag, world))
    raise TypeError(a)


def box_pow(tag: int, j: int) -> Formula:
    """The height formula □^j ⊥: 'you cannot take j steps'."""
    out: Formula = Bot()
    for _ in range(j):
        out = Box(tag, out)
    return out


# --- valuations -----------------------------------------------------------

def constant_valuation(world: int, atom: int) -> bool:
    """Every atom true everywhere: only the transition structure is observable."""
    return True


def nominal_valuation(world: int, atom: int) -> bool:
    """One atom per world: the atom p is true exactly at world p."""
    return world == atom


def binary_valuation(world: int, atom: int) -> bool:
    """Binary naming: atom p is true at m iff the p-th bit of m is set."""
    return bool((world >> atom) & 1)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  The witness frames
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

MULT = Frame.of("multiplicity", [(0, 1, 0), (0, 2, 0), (0, 3, 1), (0, 3, 2), (0, 4, 1)])
SHARE = Frame.of("shared diamond", [(0, 5, 3), (0, 5, 4), (0, 3, 1), (0, 4, 1)])
TREE = Frame.of("unravelling", [(0, 5, 3), (0, 5, 4), (0, 3, 1), (0, 4, 2)])


def chain(n: int) -> Frame:
    """The linear chain: world m+1 sees exactly world m."""
    return Frame.of("chain", [(0, m + 1, m) for m in range(n)])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Algorithm: partition refinement (bisimilarity), depth-graded
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

World = Tuple[str, int]  # (frame name, world index)


def refine(
    frames: Dict[str, Frame],
    vals: Dict[str, Valuation],
    worlds: List[World],
    atoms: int,
    rounds: int | None = None,
) -> Dict[World, int]:
    """Partition refinement computing depth-graded observational equivalence.

    Returns a map from each world to its block index.  Running to stabilization
    (``rounds=None``) yields exactly the bisimilarity classes, which by the
    Hennessy-Milner theorem are the modal-equivalence classes.  Halting after
    ``k`` rounds yields exactly the depth-``k`` equivalence classes.

    Complexity: O(rounds * |worlds| * |edges|) in this direct implementation.
    """
    tags = sorted({t for f in frames.values() for t in f.tags()})

    # round 0: atomic type
    sig0 = {w: tuple(vals[w[0]](w[1], p) for p in range(atoms)) for w in worlds}
    block = _index(sig0, worlds)

    k = 0
    while rounds is None or k < rounds:
        sig = {}
        for w in worlds:
            fname, m = w
            f = frames[fname]
            per_tag = tuple(
                tuple(sorted({block[(fname, n)] for n in f.successors(t, m)}))
                for t in tags
            )
            sig[w] = (block[w], per_tag)
        new_block = _index(sig, worlds)
        k += 1
        if rounds is None and _same_partition(block, new_block, worlds):
            return block
        block = new_block
    return block


def _index(sig: Dict[World, object], worlds: List[World]) -> Dict[World, int]:
    codes: Dict[object, int] = {}
    out: Dict[World, int] = {}
    for w in worlds:
        s = sig[w]
        if s not in codes:
            codes[s] = len(codes)
        out[w] = codes[s]
    return out


def _same_partition(a: Dict[World, int], b: Dict[World, int], worlds: List[World]) -> bool:
    for u, v in combinations(worlds, 2):
        if (a[u] == a[v]) != (b[u] == b[v]):
            return False
    return True


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Exhaustive formula enumeration (brute-force modal equivalence)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def all_formulas(layers: int, atoms: int = 1, tags: Tuple[int, ...] = (0,)) -> List[Formula]:
    """All formulas built in ``layers`` closure rounds from ⊥ and the atoms."""
    current: List[Formula] = [Bot()] + [Atom(p) for p in range(atoms)]
    for _ in range(layers):
        nxt = list(current)
        nxt += [Imp(a, b) for a in current for b in current]
        nxt += [Box(t, a) for t in tags for a in current]
        current = nxt
    return current


def separating_formulas(
    f1: Frame, v1: Valuation, m: int,
    f2: Frame, v2: Valuation, n: int,
    layers: int = 3,
    max_report: int = 3,
) -> Tuple[int, List[str]]:
    """Count formulas separating two pointed models, with a few examples."""
    seps: List[str] = []
    count = 0
    for a in all_formulas(layers):
        if sat(f1, v1, m, a) != sat(f2, v2, n, a):
            count += 1
            if len(seps) < max_report:
                seps.append(show(a))
    return count, seps


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Isomorphism of generated submodels (brute force)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def pointed_isomorphic(f1: Frame, r1: int, f2: Frame, r2: int) -> bool:
    """Is there a bijection of generated submodels matching roots and edges?"""
    A = sorted(f1.reachable(r1))
    B = sorted(f2.reachable(r2))
    if len(A) != len(B):
        return False
    tags = sorted(set(f1.tags()) | set(f2.tags()))
    rest_a = [x for x in A if x != r1]
    for perm in _permutations([x for x in B if x != r2]):
        img = {r1: r2}
        img.update(dict(zip(rest_a, perm)))
        ok = True
        for t in tags:
            e1 = {(img[m], img[n]) for m in A for n in f1.successors(t, m) if n in img}
            e2 = {(m, n) for m in B for n in f2.successors(t, m)}
            if e1 != e2:
                ok = False
                break
        if ok:
            return True
    return False


def _permutations(xs: List[int]) -> Iterable[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    if not xs:
        yield ()
        return
    for i, x in enumerate(xs):
        for rest in _permutations(xs[:i] + xs[i + 1:]):
            yield (x,) + rest


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 6.  The demonstrations
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def rule(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


def demo_multiplicity_gap() -> None:
    rule("1.  The multiplicity gap:  bisimilar, non-isomorphic, different out-degree")
    print("Frame: 1→0, 2→0, 3→1, 3→2, 4→1   (constant valuation)")
    worlds = [("M", w) for w in range(5)]
    block = refine({"M": MULT}, {"M": constant_valuation}, worlds, atoms=1)
    classes: Dict[int, List[int]] = {}
    for (_, w) in worlds:
        classes.setdefault(block[("M", w)], []).append(w)
    print(f"  bisimilarity classes         : {sorted(map(sorted, classes.values()))}")
    print(f"  3 and 4 bisimilar?           : {block[('M', 3)] == block[('M', 4)]}")
    cnt, ex = separating_formulas(MULT, constant_valuation, 3,
                                  MULT, constant_valuation, 4, layers=3)
    print(f"  separating formulas (6560)   : {cnt}")
    print(f"  out-degree of 3              : {MULT.out_degree(0, 3)}")
    print(f"  out-degree of 4              : {MULT.out_degree(0, 4)}")
    print(f"  isomorphic generated submodels? : {pointed_isomorphic(MULT, 3, MULT, 4)}")
    print("  ⇒ bisimulation invariance is STRICTLY stronger than isomorphism invariance.")
    # control
    cnt2, ex2 = separating_formulas(MULT, constant_valuation, 3,
                                    MULT, constant_valuation, 1, layers=3)
    print(f"  control (worlds 3 vs 1)      : {cnt2} separating formulas, e.g. {ex2[:2]}")


def demo_sharing_refutation() -> None:
    rule("2.  Refutation:  multiplicity does NOT close the bisimulation/iso gap")
    print("Shared diamond S : 5→3, 5→4, 3→1, 4→1        (4 reachable worlds)")
    print("Unravelling   T : 5→3, 5→4, 3→1, 4→2        (5 reachable worlds)")
    worlds = [("S", w) for w in sorted(SHARE.reachable(5))]
    worlds += [("T", w) for w in sorted(TREE.reachable(5))]
    frames = {"S": SHARE, "T": TREE}
    vals = {"S": constant_valuation, "T": constant_valuation}
    block = refine(frames, vals, worlds, atoms=1)
    print(f"  roots bisimilar?             : {block[('S', 5)] == block[('T', 5)]}")
    cnt, _ = separating_formulas(SHARE, constant_valuation, 5,
                                 TREE, constant_valuation, 5, layers=3)
    print(f"  separating formulas (6560)   : {cnt}")
    print("  out-degrees along the bisimulation:")
    matched = True
    for (fa, a) in worlds:
        for (fb, b) in worlds:
            if fa == "S" and fb == "T" and block[(fa, a)] == block[(fb, b)]:
                da, db = SHARE.out_degree(0, a), TREE.out_degree(0, b)
                print(f"      S:{a} ~ T:{b}   deg {da} vs {db}   {'ok' if da == db else 'MISMATCH'}")
                matched = matched and da == db
    print(f"  all multiplicities matched?  : {matched}")
    print(f"  reachable world counts       : |S| = {len(SHARE.reachable(5))}, "
          f"|T| = {len(TREE.reachable(5))}")
    print(f"  isomorphic generated submodels? : {pointed_isomorphic(SHARE, 5, TREE, 5)}")
    print("  ⇒ counting successors is strictly weaker than naming worlds;")
    print("    the residual invisible structure is SHARING, not multiplicity.")


def demo_depth_ladder() -> None:
    rule("3.  The depth ladder in the chain, and where it collapses")
    N = 7
    C = chain(N)
    print(f"Chain frame on worlds 0..{N}:  m+1 → m")
    print("  height formula □^j ⊥ holds at m iff m < j:")
    for j in range(1, 5):
        truth = [m for m in range(N + 1) if sat(C, constant_valuation, m, box_pow(0, j))]
        print(f"      j = {j}:  true at {truth}")
    print()
    print("  depth-k refinement: worlds k and k+1 agree at depth k, differ at depth k+1")
    worlds = [("C", w) for w in range(N + 1)]
    for k in range(0, 5):
        bk = refine({"C": C}, {"C": constant_valuation}, worlds, atoms=1, rounds=k)
        bk1 = refine({"C": C}, {"C": constant_valuation}, worlds, atoms=1, rounds=k + 1)
        same_k = bk[("C", k)] == bk[("C", k + 1)]
        same_k1 = bk1[("C", k)] == bk1[("C", k + 1)]
        print(f"      k = {k}:  depth-{k} equivalent = {same_k},  "
              f"depth-{k+1} equivalent = {same_k1}")
    print()
    print("  collapse threshold: on worlds of height ≤ k, depth-k agreement")
    print("  already implies full modal equivalence.  Heights in the chain:")
    print("      " + ", ".join(f"h({m})={C.height(m)}" for m in range(N + 1)))
    for k in range(1, 5):
        stable = refine({"C": C}, {"C": constant_valuation}, worlds, atoms=1)
        at_k = refine({"C": C}, {"C": constant_valuation}, worlds, atoms=1, rounds=k)
        lo = [w for w in worlds if C.height(w[1]) <= k]
        agree = all((at_k[u] == at_k[v]) == (stable[u] == stable[v])
                    for u, v in combinations(lo, 2))
        print(f"      k = {k}: depth-{k} partition agrees with bisimilarity "
              f"on the {len(lo)} worlds of height ≤ {k}: {agree}")


def demo_naming_budget() -> None:
    rule("4.  The naming budget:  k atoms name exactly 2^k worlds")
    print("Binary naming: atom p is true at m iff the p-th bit of m is set.")
    for k in range(1, 5):
        N = 2 ** k
        types = {tuple(binary_valuation(m, p) for p in range(k)) for m in range(N)}
        print(f"  k = {k}:  worlds 0..{N-1}  →  {len(types)} distinct atomic types "
              f"(all distinct: {len(types) == N})")
    print()
    print("Lower bound (pigeonhole): with k atoms, 2^k + 1 worlds must collide.")
    for k in range(1, 5):
        N = 2 ** k
        collision = None
        for m, n in combinations(range(N + 1), 2):
            if all(binary_valuation(m, p) == binary_valuation(n, p) for p in range(k)):
                collision = (m, n)
                break
        print(f"  k = {k}:  worlds 0..{N} — collision at {collision}")
    print()
    print("Nominal valuation (one atom per world) forces equality at depth 0:")
    for (m, n) in [(3, 4), (5, 5)]:
        eq = all(nominal_valuation(m, p) == nominal_valuation(n, p) for p in range(8))
        print(f"  worlds {m}, {n}: atomically indistinguishable = {eq}  (equal = {m == n})")
    print()
    print("With nominals, the multiplicity witness is no longer a witness:")
    cnt, ex = separating_formulas(MULT, nominal_valuation, 3,
                                  MULT, nominal_valuation, 4, layers=2)
    print(f"  worlds 3 and 4 of the multiplicity frame: {cnt} separating formulas, "
          f"e.g. {ex[:2]}")


def demo_hennessy_milner_agreement() -> None:
    rule("5.  Hennessy–Milner: refinement and formula enumeration agree everywhere")
    pairs = [
        ("M:3 vs M:4", MULT, 3, MULT, 4),
        ("M:1 vs M:2", MULT, 1, MULT, 2),
        ("M:3 vs M:1", MULT, 3, MULT, 1),
        ("M:0 vs M:1", MULT, 0, MULT, 1),
        ("S:5 vs T:5", SHARE, 5, TREE, 5),
        ("S:3 vs T:4", SHARE, 3, TREE, 4),
        ("S:1 vs T:2", SHARE, 1, TREE, 2),
        ("S:5 vs T:3", SHARE, 5, TREE, 3),
    ]
    all_ok = True
    print(f"  {'pair':<14} {'bisimilar':<11} {'separating formulas':<21} agree")
    for label, f1, m, f2, n in pairs:
        fs = {"A": f1, "B": f2}
        vs = {"A": constant_valuation, "B": constant_valuation}
        ws = [("A", w) for w in sorted(f1.reachable(m))] + \
             [("B", w) for w in sorted(f2.reachable(n))]
        blk = refine(fs, vs, ws, atoms=1)
        bis = blk[("A", m)] == blk[("B", n)]
        cnt, _ = separating_formulas(f1, constant_valuation, m,
                                     f2, constant_valuation, n, layers=3)
        ok = bis == (cnt == 0)
        all_ok = all_ok and ok
        print(f"  {label:<14} {str(bis):<11} {cnt:<21} {'✓' if ok else '✗'}")
    print(f"\n  Hennessy–Milner agreement on all tested pairs: {all_ok}")


def demo_theory_transfer() -> None:
    rule("6.  Truncated theories cannot detect sharing")
    print("The truncated theory at level N is the set of formulas valid at every")
    print("world ≤ N.  For bisimilar frames covering each other's truncations, the")
    print("two theories prove exactly the same formulas.")
    forms = all_formulas(2)
    for N in range(1, 6):
        th_s = {show(a) for a in forms
                if all(sat(SHARE, constant_valuation, m, a) for m in range(N + 1))}
        th_t = {show(a) for a in forms
                if all(sat(TREE, constant_valuation, m, a) for m in range(N + 1))}
        print(f"  N = {N}:  |Th(S)| = {len(th_s):<4} |Th(T)| = {len(th_t):<4} "
              f"equal = {th_s == th_t}")
    print("  …yet the two frames are not isomorphic. Deduction is blind to sharing.")


def main() -> None:
    print(__doc__.split("Run with:")[0].strip())
    demo_multiplicity_gap()
    demo_sharing_refutation()
    demo_depth_ladder()
    demo_naming_budget()
    demo_hennessy_milner_agreement()
    demo_theory_transfer()
    rule("Summary")
    print("  • Modal observation resolves pointed models exactly up to bisimulation.")
    print("  • Isomorphism is strictly finer; out-degree witnesses the first gap.")
    print("  • Multiplicity does NOT close the gap: the shared diamond and its")
    print("    unravelling are bisimilar, degree-matched, and non-isomorphic.")
    print("  • Naming closes it, and costs exactly ⌈log₂ N⌉ atoms.")
    print("  • Depth-k observation suffices on worlds of height ≤ k, sharply.")

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from itertools import combinations
from typing import Callable, Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Set, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Frames, valuations, formulas, semantics
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Edge = Tuple[int, int, int]  # (tag, source, target)

Valuation = Callable[[int, int], bool]  # (world, atom) -> truth value


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Frame:
    """A descending tag-indexed frame given by an explicit finite edge set.

    Only edges with ``target < source`` are retained: the descending condition
    is enforced structurally, so image-finiteness and converse well-foundedness
    hold by construction.
    """

    name: str
    edges: FrozenSet[Edge]

    @staticmethod
    def of(name: str, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> "Frame":
        kept = frozenset((i, m, n) for (i, m, n) in edges if n < m)
        return Frame(name, kept)

    def successors(self, tag: int, world: int) -> List[int]:
        """The i-successors of a world, in increasing order."""
        return sorted(n for (i, m, n) in self.edges if i == tag and m == world)

    def out_degree(self, tag: int, world: int) -> int:
        """The multiplicity-sensitive observation: number of successors."""
        return len(self.successors(tag, world))

    def tags(self) -> List[int]:
        return sorted({i for (i, _, _) in self.edges}) or [0]

    def reachable(self, root: int) -> Set[int]:
        """Worlds reachable from ``root`` along steps of arbitrary tags."""
        seen: Set[int] = {root}
        frontier = [root]
        while frontier:
            m = frontier.pop()
            for i in self.tags():
                for n in self.successors(i, m):
                    if n not in seen:
                        seen.add(n)
                        frontier.append(n)
        return seen

    def height(self, world: int) -> int:
        """Length of the longest path leaving ``world`` (bounded by ``world``)."""
        best = 0
        for i in self.tags():
            for n in self.successors(i, world):
                best = max(best, 1 + self.height(n))
        return best


# --- formulas -------------------------------------------------------------

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Bot:
    pass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Atom:
    p: int


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Imp:
    a: "Formula"
    b: "Formula"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Box:
    tag: int
    a: "Formula"


Formula = object  # one of Bot, Atom, Imp, Box


def box_depth(a: Formula) -> int:
    """Maximal nesting of boxes."""
    if isinstance(a, (Bot, Atom)):
        return 0
    if isinstance(a, Imp):
        return max(box_depth(a.a), box_depth(a.b))
    if isinstance(a, Box):
        return 1 + box_depth(a.a)
    raise TypeError(a)


def show(a: Formula) -> str:
    if isinstance(a, Bot):
        return "⊥"
    if isinstance(a, Atom):
        return f"p{a.p}"
    if isinstance(a, Imp):
        if isinstance(a.b, Bot):
            return f"¬({show(a.a)})"
        return f"({show(a.a)} → {show(a.b)})"
    if isinstance(a, Box):
        return f"□{a.tag}({show(a.a)})"
    raise TypeError(a)


def sat(frame: Frame, val: Valuation, world: int, a: Formula) -> bool:
    """Satisfaction of a formula at a world."""
    if isinstance(a, Bot):
        return False
    if isinstance(a, Atom):
        return val(world, a.p)
    if isinstance(a, Imp):
        return (not sat(frame, val, world, a.a)) or sat(frame, val, world, a.b)
    if isinstance(a, Box):
        return all(sat(frame, val, n, a.a) for n in frame.successors(a.tag, world))
    raise TypeError(a)


def box_pow(tag: int, j: int) -> Formula:
    """The height formula □^j ⊥: 'you cannot take j steps'."""
    out: Formula = Bot()
    for _ in range(j):
        out = Box(tag, out)
    return out


# --- valuations -----------------------------------------------------------

def constant_valuation(world: int, atom: int) -> bool:
    """Every atom true everywhere: only the transition structure is observable."""
    return True


def nominal_valuation(world: int, atom: int) -> bool:
    """One atom per world: the atom p is true exactly at world p."""
    return world == atom


def binary_valuation(world: int, atom: int) -> bool:
    """Binary naming: atom p is true at m iff the p-th bit of m is set."""
    return bool((world >> atom) & 1)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  The witness frames
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

MULT = Frame.of("multiplicity", [(0, 1, 0), (0, 2, 0), (0, 3, 1), (0, 3, 2), (0, 4, 1)])
SHARE = Frame.of("shared diamond", [(0, 5, 3), (0, 5, 4), (0, 3, 1), (0, 4, 1)])
TREE = Frame.of("unravelling", [(0, 5, 3), (0, 5, 4), (0, 3, 1), (0, 4, 2)])


def chain(n: int) -> Frame:
    """The linear chain: world m+1 sees exactly world m."""
    return Frame.of("chain", [(0, m + 1, m) for m in range(n)])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Algorithm: partition refinement (bisimilarity), depth-graded
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

World = Tuple[str, int]  # (frame name, world index)


def refine(
    frames: Dict[str, Frame],
    vals: Dict[str, Valuation],
    worlds: List[World],
    atoms: int,
    rounds: int | None = None,
) -> Dict[World, int]:
    """Partition refinement computing depth-graded observational equivalence.

    Returns a map from each world to its block index.  Running to stabilization
    (``rounds=None``) yields exactly the bisimilarity classes, which by the
    Hennessy-Milner theorem are the modal-equivalence classes.  Halting after
    ``k`` rounds yields exactly the depth-``k`` equivalence classes.

    Complexity: O(rounds * |worlds| * |edges|) in this direct implementation.
    """
    tags = sorted({t for f in frames.values() for t in f.tags()})

    # round 0: atomic type
    sig0 = {w: tuple(vals[w[0]](w[1], p) for p in range(atoms)) for w in worlds}
    block = _index(sig0, worlds)

    k = 0
    while rounds is None or k < rounds:
        sig = {}
        for w in worlds:
            fname, m = w
            f = frames[fname]
            per_tag = tuple(
                tuple(sorted({block[(fname, n)] for n in f.successors(t, m)}))
                for t in tags
            )
            sig[w] = (block[w], per_tag)
        new_block = _index(sig, worlds)
        k += 1
        if rounds is None and _same_partition(block, new_block, worlds):
            return block
        block = new_block
    return block


def _index(sig: Dict[World, object], worlds: List[World]) -> Dict[World, int]:
    codes: Dict[object, int] = {}
    out: Dict[World, int] = {}
    for w in worlds:
        s = sig[w]
        if s not in codes:
            codes[s] = len(codes)
        out[w] = codes[s]
    return out


def _same_partition(a: Dict[World, int], b: Dict[World, int], worlds: List[World]) -> bool:
    for u, v in combinations(worlds, 2):
        if (a[u] == a[v]) != (b[u] == b[v]):
            return False
    return True


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Exhaustive formula enumeration (brute-force modal equivalence)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def all_formulas(layers: int, atoms: int = 1, tags: Tuple[int, ...] = (0,)) -> List[Formula]:
    """All formulas built in ``layers`` closure rounds from ⊥ and the atoms."""
    current: List[Formula] = [Bot()] + [Atom(p) for p in range(atoms)]
    for _ in range(layers):
        nxt = list(current)
        nxt += [Imp(a, b) for a in current for b in current]
        nxt += [Box(t, a) for t in tags for a in current]
        current = nxt
    return current


def separating_formulas(
    f1: Frame, v1: Valuation, m: int,
    f2: Frame, v2: Valuation, n: int,
    layers: int = 3,
    max_report: int = 3,
) -> Tuple[int, List[str]]:
    """Count formulas separating two pointed models, with a few examples."""
    seps: List[str] = []
    count = 0
    for a in all_formulas(layers):
        if sat(f1, v1, m, a) != sat(f2, v2, n, a):
            count += 1
            if len(seps) < max_report:
                seps.append(show(a))
    return count, seps


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Isomorphism of generated submodels (brute force)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def pointed_isomorphic(f1: Frame, r1: int, f2: Frame, r2: int) -> bool:
    """Is there a bijection of generated submodels matching roots and edges?"""
    A = sorted(f1.reachable(r1))
    B = sorted(f2.reachable(r2))
    if len(A) != len(B):
        return False
    tags = sorted(set(f1.tags()) | set(f2.tags()))
    rest_a = [x for x in A if x != r1]
    for perm in _permutations([x for x in B if x != r2]):
        img = {r1: r2}
        img.update(dict(zip(rest_a, perm)))
        ok = True
        for t in tags:
            e1 = {(img[m], img[n]) for m in A for n in f1.successors(t, m) if n in img}
            e2 = {(m, n) for m in B for n in f2.successors(t, m)}
            if e1 != e2:
                ok = False
                break
        if ok:
            return True
    return False


def _permutations(xs: List[int]) -> Iterable[Tuple[int, ...]]:
    if not xs:
        yield ()
        return
    for i, x in enumerate(xs):
        for rest in _permutations(xs[:i] + xs[i + 1:]):
            yield (x,) + rest

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from typing import Callable, Dict, Iterable, List, Optional, Set, Tuple

Edge = Tuple[int, int, int]          # (tag, source, target)
Valuation = Callable[[int, int], bool]
World = Tuple[str, int]              # (model name, world index)


class Frame:
    """A descending frame: an edge is kept only when target < source."""

    def __init__(self, name: str, edges: Iterable[Edge]) -> None:
        self.name = name
        self.edges = frozenset((i, m, n) for (i, m, n) in edges if n < m)

    def successors(self, tag: int, world: int) -> List[int]:
        return sorted(n for (i, m, n) in self.edges if i == tag and m == world)

    def out_degree(self, tag: int, world: int) -> int:
        return len(self.successors(tag, world))

    def tags(self) -> List[int]:
        return sorted({i for (i, _, _) in self.edges}) or [0]

    def reachable(self, root: int) -> Set[int]:
        seen, stack = {root}, [root]
        while stack:
            m = stack.pop()
            for t in self.tags():
                for n in self.successors(t, m):
                    if n not in seen:
                        seen.add(n)
                        stack.append(n)
        return seen


def _index(sig: Dict[World, object], worlds: List[World]) -> Dict[World, int]:
    codes: Dict[object, int] = {}
    out: Dict[World, int] = {}
    for w in worlds:
        s = sig[w]
        if s not in codes:
            codes[s] = len(codes)
        out[w] = codes[s]
    return out


def _same(a: Dict[World, int], b: Dict[World, int], worlds: List[World]) -> bool:
    return all((a[u] == a[v]) == (b[u] == b[v]) for u, v in combinations(worlds, 2))


def refine(
    frames: Dict[str, Frame],
    valuations: Dict[str, Valuation],
    worlds: List[World],
    atoms: int = 1,
    rounds: Optional[int] = None,
) -> Dict[World, int]:
    """Return a map assigning each world its equivalence-class index.

    ``rounds=k`` gives depth-k equivalence; ``rounds=None`` iterates to a fixed
    point, giving bisimilarity.  Each round costs O(|worlds| * |edges|), and at
    most `max world index` rounds are ever needed by the collapse threshold.
    """
    tags = sorted({t for f in frames.values() for t in f.tags()})
    sig0 = {w: tuple(valuations[w[0]](w[1], p) for p in range(atoms)) for w in worlds}
    block = _index(sig0, worlds)

    k = 0
    while rounds is None or k < rounds:
        sig: Dict[World, object] = {}
        for (name, m) in worlds:
            f = frames[name]
            sig[(name, m)] = (
                block[(name, m)],
                tuple(
                    tuple(sorted({block[(name, n)] for n in f.successors(t, m)}))
                    for t in tags
                ),
            )
        new_block = _index(sig, worlds)
        k += 1
        if rounds is None and _same(block, new_block, worlds):
            return block
        block = new_block
    return block


def bisimilar(
    frames: Dict[str, Frame],
    valuations: Dict[str, Valuation],
    a: World,
    b: World,
    atoms: int = 1,
) -> bool:
    """Decide bisimilarity of two pointed models by refinement."""
    worlds = sorted(
        {(a[0], w) for w in frames[a[0]].reachable(a[1])}
        | {(b[0], w) for w in frames[b[0]].reachable(b[1])}
    )
    block = refine(frames, valuations, worlds, atoms=atoms)
    return block[a] == block[b]

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional, Set, Tuple

Edge = Tuple[int, int, int]
Valuation = Callable[[int, int], bool]


# --- syntax ---------------------------------------------------------------

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Bot:
    pass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Atom:
    p: int


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Imp:
    a: "Formula"
    b: "Formula"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Box:
    tag: int
    a: "Formula"


Formula = object

TOP: Formula = Imp(Bot(), Bot())


def neg(a: Formula) -> Formula:
    return Imp(a, Bot())


def conj(a: Formula, b: Formula) -> Formula:
    return neg(Imp(a, neg(b)))


def conj_list(xs: List[Formula]) -> Formula:
    out: Formula = TOP
    for x in reversed(xs):
        out = conj(x, out)
    return out


def diamond(tag: int, a: Formula) -> Formula:
    return neg(Box(tag, neg(a)))


def box_depth(a: Formula) -> int:
    if isinstance(a, (Bot, Atom)):
        return 0
    if isinstance(a, Imp):
        return max(box_depth(a.a), box_depth(a.b))
    if isinstance(a, Box):
        return 1 + box_depth(a.a)
    raise TypeError(a)


def show(a: Formula) -> str:
    if isinstance(a, Bot):
        return "⊥"
    if isinstance(a, Atom):
        return f"p{a.p}"
    if isinstance(a, Imp):
        return "¬" + show(a.a) if isinstance(a.b, Bot) else f"({show(a.a)} → {show(a.b)})"
    if isinstance(a, Box):
        return f"□{a.tag}{show(a.a)}"
    raise TypeError(a)


# --- semantics ------------------------------------------------------------

class Frame:
    def __init__(self, name: str, edges) -> None:
        self.name = name
        self.edges = frozenset((i, m, n) for (i, m, n) in edges if n < m)

    def successors(self, tag: int, world: int) -> List[int]:
        return sorted(n for (i, m, n) in self.edges if i == tag and m == world)

    def tags(self) -> List[int]:
        return sorted({i for (i, _, _) in self.edges}) or [0]


def sat(f: Frame, v: Valuation, w: int, a: Formula) -> bool:
    if isinstance(a, Bot):
        return False
    if isinstance(a, Atom):
        return v(w, a.p)
    if isinstance(a, Imp):
        return (not sat(f, v, w, a.a)) or sat(f, v, w, a.b)
    if isinstance(a, Box):
        return all(sat(f, v, n, a.a) for n in f.successors(a.tag, w))
    raise TypeError(a)


# --- synthesis ------------------------------------------------------------

def separate(
    f1: Frame, v1: Valuation, m: int,
    f2: Frame, v2: Valuation, n: int,
    atoms: int = 1,
) -> Optional[Formula]:
    """A formula true at (f1, m) and false at (f2, n), or None if none exists.

    Terminates because every recursive call descends strictly in at least one
    of the two frames, which are converse well-founded.
    """
    # atomic separation
    for p in range(atoms):
        if v1(m, p) and not v2(n, p):
            return Atom(p)
        if v2(n, p) and not v1(m, p):
            return neg(Atom(p))

    tags = sorted(set(f1.tags()) | set(f2.tags()))

    # forth: a successor of m matched by no successor of n
    for t in tags:
        for m2 in f1.successors(t, m):
            witnesses: List[Formula] = []
            ok = True
            for n2 in f2.successors(t, n):
                w = separate(f1, v1, m2, f2, v2, n2, atoms)
                if w is None:
                    ok = False
                    break
                witnesses.append(w)
            if ok:
                return diamond(t, conj_list(witnesses))

    # back: a successor of n matched by no successor of m; negate the dual
    for t in tags:
        for n2 in f2.successors(t, n):
            witnesses = []
            ok = True
            for m2 in f1.successors(t, m):
                w = separate(f2, v2, n2, f1, v1, m2, atoms)
                if w is None:
                    ok = False
                    break
                witnesses.append(w)
            if ok:
                return neg(diamond(t, conj_list(witnesses)))

    return None

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations
from math import ceil, log2
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Optional, Tuple

Valuation = Callable[[int, int], bool]


def binary_valuation(world: int, atom: int) -> bool:
    """Binary naming: the atom `atom` holds at `world` iff that bit is set."""
    return bool((world >> atom) & 1)


def nominal_valuation(world: int, atom: int) -> bool:
    """Nominal naming: one atom per world."""
    return world == atom


def atomic_type(v: Valuation, world: int, atoms: int) -> Tuple[bool, ...]:
    """The depth-0 observable signature of a world under `atoms` many atoms."""
    return tuple(v(world, p) for p in range(atoms))


def separates(v: Valuation, worlds: List[int], atoms: int) -> bool:
    """Does the atomic fragment with `atoms` atoms separate all these worlds?"""
    types = {atomic_type(v, w, atoms) for w in worlds}
    return len(types) == len(worlds)


def find_collision(v: Valuation, worlds: List[int], atoms: int) -> Optional[Tuple[int, int]]:
    """The first pair of distinct worlds with the same atomic type, if any."""
    seen: Dict[Tuple[bool, ...], int] = {}
    for w in worlds:
        t = atomic_type(v, w, atoms)
        if t in seen:
            return (seen[t], w)
        seen[t] = w
    return None


def required_budget(n_worlds: int) -> int:
    """ceil(log2 n_worlds): the exact number of atoms needed to name n worlds."""
    return 0 if n_worlds <= 1 else ceil(log2(n_worlds))


def verify_threshold(k: int) -> Tuple[bool, bool]:
    """Check both halves of the threshold theorem at budget `k`.

    Returns (sufficiency, necessity):
      sufficiency -- binary naming separates 0..2^k - 1 with k atoms;
      necessity   -- no valuation with k atoms separates 0..2^k (pigeonhole),
                     checked here against binary naming and a random-free

    n = 2 ** k
    sufficiency = separates(binary_valuation, list(range(n)), k)
    necessity = find_collision(binary_valuation, list(range(n + 1)), k) is not None
    return sufficiency, necessity

def chain_successors(m: int) -> List[int]:
    return [m - 1] if m >= 1 else []


def chain_refinement_sizes(n: int, max_rounds: int) -> List[int]:
    """Number of still-identified unordered pairs after k rounds, k = 0..max."""
    worlds = list(range(n + 1))
